Nasa Internship
Allison Bond

Mike Jung spent summer 2006 in Florida, but he was no beach bum.  Instead, the Weinberg sophomore kept busy with a NASA-sponsored internship through the Space and Lunar Sciences and Technology Program at Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Fla.

Jung, who was one of 22 program interns from around the country, had the chance to do hands-on research through The Spaceflight and Lunar Sciences and Technology Program.  The internship entailed planning an experiment protocol, conducting research and analyzing the results.  Jung presented his project about motion sickness to staff and other interns and also had the opportunity to attend professional workshops and lectures on a variety of NASA operations, from environmental conservation to astronomy.

Jung, a biological sciences and economics double major, says he learned not only about his specific research topic, but also about the science community and research in general.  “When you pursue something [in research],” he says, “you need to really set your direction, because there are so many things you could look at. You need to use your resources efficiently, and having a focus helps you do that.”

Jung also says he got plenty of experience with writing and executing research protocols.  “I learned a lot about the details of research,” he says. “There are small nuances you wouldn’t think of [when planning a project], such as fitting your tests into your subjects’ schedules.”  Another perk of the program was getting to know the other interns, he says, all of whom were highly intelligent and motivated.  “Everyone was like-minded, hard-working and bright,” he says.  “I wouldn’t be surprised if I saw them in extremely influential positions in the future.”

Jung heard about the internship from friend and fraternity brother Weinberg senior Nirav Shah, who took part in the internship in summer 2005 and gave the program glowing reviews.  “It was one of the best times I’ve ever had,” Shah says, citing his favorite aspect of the program as “being at [NASA’s] Kennedy Space Center every day, doing things we had only dreamed of and…meeting people most people never will,” he says. “Oh yeah, and getting to watch the Return to Flight [mission’s space shuttle Discovery] from ringside seats.”

In addition to designing and performing research, the summer 2006 interns found time to volunteer at a beach cleanup and a senior center and also went skydiving, played beach volleyball and saw a NASA shuttle launch in Miami.  Jung says activities like these helped create a fun, friendly atmosphere among the students. “It brought all these interns together who have a very strong interest in science to collaborate and hang out together,” Jung says. “There was a really strong sense of community.”

Unfortunately, the specific internship program Shah and Jung took part in has been discontinued. The main culprit: budget cuts, Shah says.  “The Bush administration wants NASA to go to the moon, Mars and beyond with the same budget they have now,” he says.  “Something’s got to go, right?”  There are still plenty of internships available, however, including 10 through NASA for university students, such as the Undergraduate Student Research Program and the Career Exploration Program.  Other governmental organizations, like the National Institutes of Health, also have summer internship programs. Applications are generally due between November and January, and since they often require letters of recommendations or essays, it’s best to start filling out the forms early.

Overall, Jung and Shah say an internship in science is a great way to gain knowledge and meet other motivated students.  The two were also thrilled to spend time with some of the world’s most influential scientists. “These are the people that put a man on the moon and are building The International Space Station,” Shah says.  “It blows your mind sometimes when you think about the fact that you were there, you met them and you’ve seen what they do. In some way, you were a part of it for awhile.”

RESEARCH
The Effects of Inspiratory Resistance on Motion Sickness and its Hemodynamics
Michael Jung
DEPARTMENT OF BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING
Richard Ha
ADVISOR,
THE OHIO STATE UNIVERSITY
Dave R. Bush, Don F. Doerr, Kenneth D. Cohen
ADVISORS,
NASA BIOMEDICAL, KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, FL

A common source of discomfort for many, the study of motion sickness carries notable importance for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) as it is an issue that affects a number of its most important human resources, including its astronauts, aviators, and sailors.

Previous studies have shown that cerebral hypoperfusion (reductions in cerebral blood flow) precedes the onset of motion sickness and that inspiratory resistance (resistance to breathing in) is an effective treatment in maintaining cerebral bloodflow.  Our experiment investigated if the application of inspiratory resistance through an inspiratory Impedance Threshold Device™ (ITD) mitigated motion sickness symptoms through the prevention of motion sickness-induced decreases in cerebral bloodflow.  In the initial part of our study we constructed an improved off vertical axis rotation (OVAR) chair in order to collect real-time physiological data on a computer system contained within the chair.  After chair construction we began studying this potential countermeasure to motion sickness.  Three males and 3 females susceptible to motion sickness were observed during OVAR while breathing through either an active ITD or control SHAM.  Though further studies are necessary for more conclusive findings, the resulting data from this preliminary experiment showed that the ITD did not appear to significantly mitigate motion sickness symptoms, but was shown to maintain cerebral bloodflow.  The findings from this study indicate that reductions in cerebral bloodflow may be a physiological variable correlated with, but not an underlying cause, of motion sickness.

Motion sickness is defined as nausea caused by motion, described by Serrador et al. as “a persistent unpleasant sensation that may be felt in the stomach, upper abdominal area, and especially the esophagus or throat.” ¹  Its physiological causes are still debated.  Several countermeasures used by astronauts that experience motion sickness include resting for several days upon entering microgravity (“outer space”) and use of medication.  Resting upon entry into microgravity consumes valuable space-time.  Use of medication to mitigate motion sickness can result in unwanted side effects such as drowsiness and negative reactions with other drugs.  Medication may also have varying efficacies in microgravity, so extended precaution is necessary for its use in the mitigation of motion sickness.  A non-pharmaceutical treatment of motion sickness, such as inspiratory resistance, may improve the safety and efficiency of motion sickness mitigation.

A previous study by Serrador et al. has shown that reductions in cerebral bloodflow, quantified by measurement of the directly-related cerebral bloodflow velocity (CBFV), precede the development of moderate motion sickness.¹  The inspiratory Impedance Threshold Device™ is a small, plastic valve-like device placed in the mouth that provides resistance only to inspiration (Figure 1).  Previous studies by Convertino et al. have demonstrated the effectiveness of the ITD in increasing CBFV when subjects used the device.  The ITD generates a greater negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration which enhances venous return of blood to the heart and lungs, consequently increasing the amount of blood pumped by the heart to the brain and body.²
Figure 1.  The ITD (with mouthpiece) is a compact, plastic valve that provides resistance to inspiration.
